`fastapi/sse.py` defines `ServerSentEvent` and `format_sse_event`, which build the wire bytes. `fastapi/routing.py` turns each yielded item into those bytes during streaming.

The bytes are written in this order, one field per line, with the event closed by a blank line:

```
: <comment line>            (one per line of comment, if set)
event: <name>               (if set)
data: <line 1>              (one per line of the payload, if set)
data: <line 2>
id: <id>                    (if set)
retry: <ms>                 (if set)
<blank line>
```

So a multi-line payload `"a\nb"` with `retry=3000` and a comment becomes `: note\ndata: a\ndata: b\nretry: 3000\n\n`. The payload is JSON-encoded unless `raw_data` is used. Also, empty `data` produces no `data:` line, since `splitlines()` returns nothing.

Outermost to innermost, the stack is `ServerErrorMiddleware`, then the user-registered middlewares in the order they were added (first added is outermost), then `ExceptionMiddleware`, then `AsyncExitStackMiddleware`, then the router. This is built in `build_middleware_stack`, which wraps the router by iterating the middleware list in reverse.

`AsyncExitStackMiddleware` sits innermost, just outside the router, so that the file-closing stack is created inside the user middlewares. The code comment says this is because user middlewares run in a new contextvars copy (via anyio task groups), so placing the stack there keeps it in the same context as the handler. Because it is also inside `ExceptionMiddleware`, an exception from the route unwinds through it and closes the files before the exception handler produces a response. **Order, outermost to innermost** (`fastapi/applications.py:1035-1067`):

1. `ServerErrorMiddleware` (the 500 handler)
2. User-registered middlewares (`self.user_middleware`, in the order they were added)
3. `ExceptionMiddleware` (the registered exception handlers)
4. `AsyncExitStackMiddleware` (closes uploaded files)
5. `self.router` (the request dispatcher)

`build_middleware_stack` wraps the router by iterating the list in reverse, so the first entry ends up outermost.

**Why the file-closing layer is innermost:** the code comment says it must come after the user middlewares. Those middlewares can start a new contextvars copy through an AnyIO task group, so a stack placed outside them would not see the same context the endpoint runs in. Placing it just outside the router keeps it in the endpoint's context and closes uploaded files as soon as the handler and response finish, before any exception or user-middleware unwinding. The "closes files" job also no longer needs to be there for dependencies, which now use their own `AsyncExitStack` (`fastapi/routing.py`). The comment itself says the contextvars reason is "not strictly necessary" for closing files, so that part is a design preference rather than a hard requirement.
